title: Process-Integrated Determination of the Material Properties of Thin-Walled Die-Cast Components
abstract: Abstract Conventional characterization of die-cast components relies on destructive tests that are performed after casting and often require separate specimens, limiting their representativeness of the finished part. This work explores shearing as a process-integrated method for extracting material information. Force–displacement curves recorded during shearing were evaluated for aluminum and magnesium die-cast alloys and compared with tensile tests and computed tomography (CT) measurements. The peak shearing force scaled with tensile strength, the post-peak displacement reflected ductility, and a reduced mechanical work of the curve indicated elevated volumetric defects. The shearing force signals exhibited high repeatability and reproduced the material trends from tensile and CT data. The study demonstrates that shearing can provide a compact, inline, and nondestructive means of monitoring strength, ductility, and defect content in die-cast production.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Thin-walled die-cast components are widely used in automotive, aerospace, and consumer applications due to their high strength-to-weight ratio and production efficiency. Ensuring the consistent quality of these components is challenging, as their mechanical performance strongly depends on microstructure, alloy composition, and casting conditions. Conventional material characterization methods, such as tensile and hardness testing, provide detailed information on mechanical properties but are typically destructive, time-consuming, and often limited in representativeness for the final component.

Process-integrated approaches that enable material evaluation during production can detect variations in strength, ductility, and defects earlier, reducing scrap rates and improving overall process control. However, existing inline monitoring techniques are mostly limited to process parameters such as temperature, pressure, or melt composition, and do not directly assess mechanical properties. This study addresses this gap by investigating whether features extracted from sprue and flash shearing can provide meaningful indicators of material behavior, laying the foundation for inline, nondestructive quality assessment.

sections.heading: State of Research
paragraphs: Material characterization plays a central role in the development and quality assurance of metallic materials. In particular, the properties of material failure and plasticity are decisive for the mechanical behavior of components. The characterization of these properties is carried out using various standardized methods, both surface-oriented and volumetric.

sections.heading: Standardized Test Methods
paragraphs: Material failure describes the resistance of a material to plastic deformation and fracture under mechanical load. The most important test methods include the tensile test in accordance with DIN EN ISO 6892-1, corresponding to ASTM E8/E8M, which determines mechanical parameters such as yield strength and tensile strength, and the Brinell hardness test in accordance with DIN EN ISO 6506, corresponding to ASTM E10, which correlates indirectly with strength. 1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 – 5

Plasticity describes the plastic deformability of a material before it fractures. It is determined using a tensile test in accordance with DIN EN ISO 6892-1, which provides the elongation at fracture as a primary indicator of a material’s plastic deformability. Volumetric defects significantly affect the mechanical properties of materials. To characterize the pore structure, industrial X-ray computed tomography, as outlined in the German Foundry Association guideline P203, enables nondestructive, three-dimensional analysis of pore distributions and sizes. 6

Near-surface testing methods such as hardness testing in accordance with DIN EN ISO 6506 provide quick assessments of mechanical properties but are often only partially representative of the entire component volume. 3 , 5  Volumetric methods, such as CT analysis according to DIN EN ISO 15708, corresponding to ASTM E1441 and tensile tests, provide more comprehensive information on the material structure and its influence on mechanical properties. 7 , 8

Alongside CT, conventional radiographic testing is widely used to detect internal discontinuities in aluminum and magnesium die castings. ASTM E505 defines standardized reference radiographs with graded severity levels for typical defects such as porosity, cold fill, and shrinkage, enabling a fast two-dimensional, comparison-based assessment, but without quantitative three-dimensional information on defect volume or morphology. 9
The combination of surface and volumetric methods ensures a holistic evaluation of the material properties and promotes quality assurance in industrial applications.

sections.heading: Testing Procedures in Production Processes
paragraphs: Since quality control and quality assurance are closely linked to material characterization, a number of testing procedures affect the entire production process. The testing procedures range from process monitoring to the final inspection of the manufactured components. This includes continuous data recording from melting, molding, and casting systems to ensure reliable, consistent process control. The test criteria vary depending on the product and include visual inspections of the inner and outer surfaces, dimensional inspections with measuring machines, nondestructive testing, and hardness testing of the zones close to the surface, and testing for blowholes, pores, and cracks by X-ray analysis and computed tomography. Material characterization in die-casting can be approached at different stages of the process, namely before, during, and after casting.

Selected Preprocess Material Characterization Emission spectral analysis  Determines the material composition by means of characteristic wavelengths in the optical spectrum, induced by spark discharges, electric arcs, or lasers. 10 Temperature monitoring of the melt  Continuous measurement of melt temperature using multiple measurement points and control devices for process regulation. 11 Selected In-Process Material Characterization Casting pressure measurement  Monitoring of hydraulic pressure, which influences melt flow velocity and is used for analyzing mold filling. 11 Temperature distribution in the die-casting mold  Recording of temperature distribution along the mold wall to determine the solidification time. 12 Selected Post-Process Material Characterization Light microscopy  Optical analysis of specimen surfaces to identify microstructural features. 13 Electron microscopy  High-resolution imaging techniques (TEM and SEM) for surface and microstructural analysis. 13 Tensile testing  Mechanical testing to determine strength and deformation properties. 13 Charpy impact test  Evaluation of the toughness of metallic materials using a drop-weight hammer. 13 Hardness testing  Determination of a material’s resistance to plastic deformation. 13 Rotating bending test  Assessment of fatigue strength of round specimens under cyclic loading. 14 Liquid penetrant testing  Detection of fine surface cracks using capillary effects. 13 Eddy current testing  Identification of material defects through variations in electrical coupling. 13 Radiographic inspection with X-rays and gamma rays  Imaging methods for detecting internal defects. 13 Ultrasonic testing  Analysis of material homogeneity by reflection of sound waves at internal boundaries. 13 While established material testing methods enable a detailed characterization of the mechanical properties of metallic materials, their applicability in industrial production is limited by high time consumption and the destructive nature of the tests. This is particularly critical for thin-walled die-cast components, where conventional testing methods are not suitable for immediate quality control, thereby motivating the development of process-integrated characterization approaches.

X-ray computed tomography (CT) provides comprehensive three-dimensional insights into internal defect structures in aluminum cast alloys. For instance, Mathew et al. 15  investigated the influence of air melting and vacuum induction melting on porosity formation in Al–7Si alloys using CT and correlated porosity characteristics with tensile properties, demonstrating the capability of CT to link processing conditions with mechanical behavior. Despite its high descriptive power, CT remains a post-process, cost, and time-intensive technique, limiting its suitability for inline quality assurance in high-volume die-casting production.

A previously unaddressed concept in the literature is  shearing , which could enable both mechanical characterization and efficient inline monitoring of material properties by leveraging the shearing process within the die-casting production chain.

As part of a literature review, experimental setups outside the field of casting were analyzed that were equipped with measurement systems potentially transferable to process-integrated material characterization through shearing of die-cast components. This resulted in a collection of ten setups (I–X), described and evaluated based on a total of twelve research studies, as listed in Table  1 . Table 1 Overview of the Investigated Experimental Setups and Research Studies Setup Experimental Setup Investigated Research Studies I Piezoelectric force measurement above the punch 16 ,  17 – 18 II Comparison of force measurement using strain gauges and piezoelectric sensors at different punch positions and below the die 19 III Piezoelectric force measurement above the punch and below the die 20 IV Piezoelectric force measurement using transverse dowels in a rotary cutting system 21 V Piezoelectric cutting and transverse force measurement in the punch block 22 VI Piezoelectric force measurement at upper and lower dies, as well as acceleration measurement 23 VII Force measurement using strain-gauge rosettes on the punch surface 24 VIII Local force measurement using strain-gauge rosettes along the cutting edge 25 IX Development of thin-film force sensors for use in cutting tools 26 X Temperature measurement of the shearing zone 27

The investigated measurement principles of the experimental setups are illustrated in a morphological box in Figure  1 . Force measurement is predominantly realized using piezoelectric load cells with an integrated punch. Position measurement is most commonly performed using laser distance sensors, although a variety of techniques have been reported in the literature. Acceleration measurements are only rarely applied. The temperature in the shearing zone can be determined by measuring the thermoelectric voltage using the Seebeck effect. 27 Figure 1 Morphological box of common shearing measurement principles.

The central research gap lies in the quantitative correlation between the force–displacement curves of the shearing process and the major material parameters, such as material failure and plasticity. The following chapter describes preliminary tests that systematically investigate these correlations and evaluate the potential of the process.

sections.heading: Material
paragraphs: An initial series of preliminary tests was conducted to establish a consistent experimental basis for the subsequent investigations. Different die-cast materials were selected and examined under identical shearing process parameters to ensure comparability between experiments.

The test specimens were manufactured from existing die-cast plates using waterjet cutting. This manufacturing route allows precise specimen geometries while avoiding thermal influence on material properties. Figure  2  illustrates the geometry of the specimens used for the shearing experiments. Figure 2 Geometry of the shearing tests (left) and sampling points from the die-cast plate (right).

Table  2  lists the six different material configurations (ZS1–ZS6) tested, which differed in their alloy composition, heat-treatment conditions, and casting process. The series includes both conventionally cast and vacuum-cast aluminum alloys in the heat-treatment conditions F, T5, and T7. The sample designation follows the scheme ZS1-X-Y, where ZS1 indicates the specific alloy composition. The subsequent number (1–5) denotes the casting plate from which the sample was taken, and the final letter (A–E) specifies the exact location within that plate. A complete sample designation is, therefore, for example, ZS1-1-A. Fifteen samples were prepared for each of the six material configurations to ensure a meaningful database.

The conventional material characterization was carried out by tensile tests. These tests serve as a basis for comparison and enable the determination of properties such as tensile strength, yield strength, and elongation at break.

sections.heading: Shearing Tool
paragraphs: Subsequently, the samples were cut in the modular shearing tool illustrated in Figure  3 . A symmetric, closed-cutting geometry was used, in which the punch separates the material within the specific shearing zone. To fix the specimen during shearing, a blank-holder force was applied using clamping plates. This configuration creates a three-dimensional stress and strain state across the specimen width. Figure 3 Tool in bottom dead center position.

sections.heading: Universal Testing Machine
Computed Tomography
paragraphs: To detect volumetric defects, such as pores and blowholes, prior to mechanical testing, the specimens were analyzed using an industrial X-ray computed tomography system (METROTOM 1500, Carl Zeiss AG, Oberkochen, Germany). 29  The samples were arranged in a circular fixture to allow for simultaneous scanning of multiple specimens, ensuring consistent scanning parameters across the batch. Figure  4  illustrates the mounting of the samples inside the CT scanner (Figure  4 a) and the corresponding 3D reconstruction (Figure  4 b).

This nondestructive analysis allowed for the mapping of internal defects within the shearing zone. The resulting volumetric data were used to correlate the presence of volumetric defects with the specific characteristics of the force–displacement curves recorded during the subsequent shearing process. Figure 4 Experimental setup for the computed tomography analysis performed prior to shearing to identify volumetric defects.

sections.heading: Surface Topography Measurement
paragraphs: The cut surfaces resulting from the shearing tests were additionally characterized using a tactile stylus measurement system (MarSurf XC 20, Mahr GmbH, Göttingen, Germany) in combination with a contour feed unit (PCV 200). 30  The measurement is based on a diamond stylus scanning the surface, while the vertical deflection is recorded to determine the surface topography.

sections.heading: Material Failure
paragraphs: The similarity between trends in tensile and shearing configurations demonstrates that the maximum shearing force scales with the alloy’s macroscopic flow stress. Although the stress state during shearing combines compressive, shearing, and tensile components, the observed correlation indicates that the peak force can serve as a reliable process-integrated proxy for tensile strength. This correspondence suggests that local variations in hardness or microstructural condition, arising from casting parameters or heat treatment, can be detected directly during shearing without destructive testing. Figure 5 Comparison of shearing and tensile tests of the aluminum alloy AlSi10MnMg in the heat-treated conditions T5 (ZS5) and T7 (ZS6). The diagram illustrates the differences in the mechanical behavior of both conditions, particularly with regard to strength and deformation properties under shearing and tensile loading.

sections.heading: Plasticity
paragraphs: Differences in the post-peak region of the force–displacement curves reflect the material’s deformation and fracture behavior. The ZS6 alloy in the T7 condition exhibits a larger displacement to failure under both tensile and shearing loading compared with ZS5 (T5), consistent with its reduced strength and enhanced plastic deformability after overaging. The smoother, less abrupt force drop in the shearing curve of ZS6 indicates a more gradual crack propagation and energy absorption before separation, whereas the sharp decline for ZS5 corresponds to a more brittle fracture response.

These findings underline that the displacement to failure extracted from the shearing signal provides a qualitative measure of ductility. The strong agreement between tensile and shearing-based trends confirms that the shearing process captures not only strength-related effects but also the material’s capacity for plastic deformation. This sensitivity makes the method suitable for distinguishing between microstructural states with varying toughness or aging conditions.

The material property volumetric defects correlated with the overall force–displacement curve, where a lower magnitude of the total curve indicated higher volumetric defects. CT scans taken before the shearing process revealed volumetric defects in the separation zone. In Figure  6  is an example curve for the material configuration ZS3. Two of the samples, ZS3-3-B and ZS3-3-C, exhibited pronounced volumetric defects. These material defects significantly affect the maximum load that can be sustained during shearing before the sample fails. Additionally, material failure is delayed, seemingly due to the compaction of free volume in the region of volumetric defects. Figure 6 Influence of volumetric defects on the force–displacement curve of shearing tests for the magnesium alloy MgAl4Si (ZS3). The presented curves illustrate the relationship between defect content and mechanical behavior, particularly the maximum shearing force.

sections.heading: Cut-Surface Partitioning and Shearing-Work Distribution
paragraphs: For all investigated material configurations, fracture formation accounts for the largest share of the total shearing work. This indicates that final separation is predominantly governed by crack initiation and propagation. The relative partitioning of the shearing work differs noticeably between the material states and therefore provides additional information on the underlying separation behavior.

The fracture contribution ranges from approximately 56% for ZS1 to 79% for ZS3. In contrast, the burnished zone contribution varies between about 9% and 23%, while the edge-indentation contribution lies between approximately 12% and 22%. These differences indicate that the material configurations do not primarily differ in whether fracture occurs, but rather in the extent to which stable plastic shearing precedes final crack-controlled separation.

ZS3 exhibits the highest fracture contribution and the lowest burnished zone share. This indicates a strongly fracture-dominated separation process with only a limited phase of stable shearing prior to final failure. By contrast, ZS6 exhibits the highest burnished zone contribution and a comparatively lower fracture share, pointing to a more extended stable shearing phase before separation. This observation is consistent with the higher plastic deformability discussed in the previous sections. ZS1 is characterized by nearly equal contributions from edge indentation and burnished zone, suggesting a comparatively balanced transition from initial local deformation to stable shearing.

sections.heading: Correlation Between Shearing and Tensile Force
paragraphs: Based on this comparison, a linear regression analysis was performed using the peak shearing force and peak tensile force for each specimen. The resulting relationships are presented in Figure  9 . For all investigated alloys, the data indicate positive linear trends between peak shearing force and peak tensile force. The degree of correlation varies between the alloy states. ZS1, ZS4, and ZS6 exhibit high coefficients of determination, whereas ZS2, ZS3, and ZS5 exhibit lower, but still positive, correlations.

In addition to the force-based comparison, Figure  10  provides the stress–strain curves derived from both shearing and tensile tests for all investigated material configurations. For all alloy states, the curves obtained from both methods indicate similar qualitative progressions with increasing strain. At the same time, the stress levels derived from the shearing tests are higher than those obtained from the tensile tests. The relative differences between the investigated alloy states are visible in both representations.

sections.heading: Discussion
paragraphs: The results indicate that characteristic features of the shearing force–displacement signal contain material information that is qualitatively consistent with conventional characterization methods, even though the stress state in shearing differs fundamentally from that in tensile testing. In particular, the comparison of AlSi10MnMg in the T5 and T7 conditions (Figure  5 ) demonstrates that the shearing response is sensitive to microstructural condition and heat-treatment state. The higher peak force observed for the T5 condition and the larger displacement to failure observed for the T7 condition follow the same material trend as in the tensile tests, indicating that the shearing signal reflects both strength-related and ductility-related behavior.

This interpretation is further supported by the stress–strain curves for ZS6 in Figure  10 , which compares the stress–strain responses derived from tensile and shearing experiments for AlSi10MnMg in the T7 condition. Both testing methods exhibit comparable qualitative trends in hardening behavior, while the shear response reaches higher apparent stress levels due to the different stress state during shearing. The agreement in trend therefore supports the assumption that the shearing process captures relevant aspects of the mechanical material response. However, the absolute values cannot be interpreted in the same way as under uniaxial tensile loading.

Further support for this interpretation is provided by the evaluation of cut-surface characteristics and shearing work. By partitioning the total shearing work into edge indentation, burnished zone, and fracture formation, additional insight into the prevailing separation mechanisms is obtained. In particular, the relative contributions of the burnished zone and fracture formation indicate whether material behavior is dominated by stable plastic shearing or by earlier crack-controlled failure. This complements the force–displacement analysis and supports the conclusion that the shearing operation contains direct information on material failure and plasticity. Furthermore, CT analysis before shearing enabled the identification of volumetric defects in the later separation zone, linking reduced force–displacement levels and shearing work to elevated defect content.

A similar conclusion follows from the correlation analysis between peak shearing force and peak tensile force. The regression analysis in Figure  9  exhibits a positive linear relationship between peak shearing force and peak tensile force across all investigated alloy states. However, the strength of this relationship differs between the materials. ZS1, ZS4, and ZS6 exhibit high coefficients of determination, whereas ZS2, ZS3, and ZS5 indicate lower, but still positive, correlations. Because of the fundamentally different loading conditions, a direct one-to-one correspondence cannot be expected. Nevertheless, the observed trends indicate that higher peak shearing forces are generally associated with higher tensile forces. Peak shearing force can therefore be interpreted as a promising strength-related indicator, but not as a universal quantitative substitute for tensile testing. Instead, the results suggest that alloy-specific or condition-specific calibration may be required for a more quantitative interpretation.

In addition to strength and ductility, the shearing signal also appears sensitive to volumetric defects. Samples with pronounced defects in the separation zone exhibited reduced overall force–displacement responses and lower maximum loads. At the same time, CT observations support the interpretation that these deviations are linked to internal defects (Figure  6 ). Rather than proving a universal defect metric, the present results indicate that characteristic changes in the overall curve shape and magnitude can serve as qualitative indicators of elevated defect content. Blistering, in contrast, was observed only very sporadically in the T7 plates (approximately 1 out of 15 plates) and occurred exclusively in the gating/trim region or in the overflow region. As these areas lie outside the locations from which shear and tensile specimens were extracted, the observed blisters did not affect the measured mechanical properties.

The different deformation and failure mechanisms of both test methods can explain this lower scatter. In tensile testing, the measured displacement reflects the global deformation of the entire gauge length and is therefore more sensitive to local inhomogeneities such as pores or microstructural variations. In contrast, the shearing process is governed by a localized separation zone with well-defined boundary conditions. Failure occurs through localized shear fracture rather than progressive global damage, thereby reducing the influence of specimen-to-specimen variations on the overall force–displacement response. This contributes to the robustness and repeatability of the shearing signal under controlled conditions and supports its potential suitability for inline monitoring during an already required shearing operation.

At the same time, the shearing response is inherently process-dependent. Parameters such as clearance, punch and die radii, blank-holder force, shearing path, and shearing speed influence the measured signal. In the present study, only one fixed parameter set and quasi-static loading conditions were considered, and the specimens were extracted from plate material. The relation between overflow-based testing and actual part quality is complex. The current observations are therefore limited to the investigated geometry, material states, and process window. Further investigations are required to systematically assess the transferability of the method to a broader range of component geometries, thicknesses, and industrial operating conditions. Figure 11 Force–displacement curves for shearing and tensile tests of the aluminum alloy AlSi10MnMg in the heat-treated condition T7 (ZS6). The shearing tests exhibit lower variability than the tensile tests, indicating higher repeatability under shear loading.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This work establishes shearing as a compact, process-integrated approach for extracting material-relevant information from thin-walled die-cast alloys without the need for elaborate specimen preparation. Experimental results demonstrate that characteristic features of the force–displacement curves obtained during shearing replicate the qualitative trends observed in conventional tensile testing and computed tomography. This enables assessment of material failure, plasticity, and volumetric defect sensitivity directly during the required shearing operation.

In particular, the peak shearing force correlates with tensile strength, while the displacement to failure indicates plastic deformability. A reduction in the mechanical work is associated with elevated volumetric defects in the separation zone. The consistently low scatter of the shearing signals further underscores the method’s robustness and repeatability under controlled conditions, supporting its potential suitability for inline material monitoring in die-casting production.

Future research will focus on extending the approach toward industrially relevant boundary conditions. This will include the development of an optimized specimen geometry to ensure the representativeness of the results. The aim is to replicate the process fluctuations that occur in industrial settings on a laboratory scale. In parallel, the quantitative correlation analysis between tensile and shearing test results will be further investigated. In addition, a dedicated shearing machine tailored to this application is planned. The shearing tool will include an appropriate metrological verification, such as high-speed imaging of the shearing zone to resolve local strain and damage evolution, where digital image correlation (DIC) and optical flow techniques provide quantitative mapping of deformation and fracture in the shearing region, enabling independent validation of process signals and deeper insight into ductility and defect sensitivity. DIC enables full-field displacement measurement by tracking stochastic surface patterns between successive high-speed images. From the resulting displacement fields, local strain and strain-rate distributions can be derived, allowing identification of strain localization and crack initiation within the shear zone. In addition, spatiotemporal optical flow provides dense, pixel-wise velocity fields based on the brightness constancy and motion continuity assumptions. This approach is particularly suited to resolving highly localized, rapid fracture processes, such as crack propagation during separation. The combination of both methods allows a quantitative mapping of local deformation mechanisms and their direct correlation with characteristic features of the force–displacement signal. 31  Another aim is to measure the temperature evolution in the shearing zone by exploiting the Seebeck effect so that the shearing element itself functions as a thermoelectric sensor, enabling direct in-process acquisition of the local thermal history. 27  Overall, these developments aim to deepen the physical understanding of the shearing process and to further evaluate its potential as a reliable process-integrated material characterization method for thin-walled die-cast components.
